title: Filtered Indexes for Rare-Value Queries
description: A filtered index over just the rows a query cares about is tiny and fast, avoiding a scan of a mostly-irrelevant table. Why it matters: most tables have a small "active"/"pending"/"error" subset that gets queried constantly -- filtered indexes are an underused, high-value technique for exactly that shape of workload.
narrative:
## What This Lesson Is About

This lesson is about a simple but very common shape of query: "give me the few rows that matter out of a huge pile of mostly-irrelevant ones." Think of orders that are `Pending` out of a table where 99% of rows are already `Shipped` or `Delivered`, or support tickets that are `Open` when almost everything is `Closed`. The interesting/urgent rows are always a tiny sliver of the table, but the table itself might have hundreds of thousands or millions of rows total.

You'd expect that putting a normal index on the `Status` column would fix this — and it does help in general, but there's a subtlety. A regular (non-filtered) index on `Status` has to contain an entry for *every single row in the table*, including all those `Shipped`/`Delivered`/`Closed` rows you never actually query for. It's still much smaller than the full table (since it might only store the `Status` value plus a pointer to the row), but it's not nearly as small as it could be. And more importantly, if `Status` only has a handful of distinct values (say, 5 possible statuses across 400,000 rows), the optimizer (the part of SQL Server that decides how to execute your query) often looks at that index and reasons: "if I use this index to find all the `Pending` rows, and roughly 1/5th of the table matches each value on average, that's still a lot of rows — cheaper to just scan the whole table once than to do a lot of index lookups." This is a really important, generalizable idea in SQL Server tuning: **an index is not automatically used just because it exists on the column you're filtering by.** The optimizer estimates cost based on how selective the predicate is — meaning, what fraction of the table actually matches — and for common values, it may reject the index entirely in favor of a scan.

So what's the actual fix? SQL Server lets you build a **filtered index** — an index that only contains rows matching a condition you specify, using a `WHERE` clause right in the `CREATE INDEX` statement itself (e.g. `CREATE INDEX IX_Orders_Pending ON Orders(OrderDate) WHERE Status = 'Pending'`). Instead of an index over the whole 400,000-row table, you get an index over just the ~4,000 `Pending` rows. This is a completely different situation from the optimizer's point of view: the index is now tiny, and it *only* contains the rows you actually care about, so a query filtering on `Status = 'Pending'` (matched exactly by the filter definition) can use it as a small, cheap, focused structure rather than something diluted by 396,000 irrelevant rows.

Here's the mental model that helps this click: imagine a phone book for an entire country, versus a separate little card file that only has the phone numbers of people who currently owe you money. If you're always looking up "who owes me money," you don't want to page through the giant national phone book (even if it's alphabetically sorted and technically "indexed") — you want the small, purpose-built card file that only has the handful of relevant entries. A filtered index is that purpose-built card file: small enough to fit almost entirely in memory, fast to scan even in the worst case, and exactly matched to the query pattern that matters.

There's a practical constraint worth knowing: a filtered index is only useful for queries whose predicate matches (or is a subset of) the index's filter condition. If your filtered index only covers `Status = 'Pending'`, a query asking for `Status = 'Shipped'` gets no help from it at all — you'd need a different index (possibly another filtered index) for that. This is why filtered indexes work best for the specific, well-known "the rare/urgent subset" pattern rather than as a general-purpose index.

Why does this matter in the real world? Because "the interesting rows are a tiny fraction of a huge table" is an extremely common production shape: pending work items, failed jobs, active sessions, unread notifications, in-progress transactions. These are exactly the queries that get hit over and over again by dashboards and background jobs, so they're worth optimizing specifically rather than relying on a general index and hoping the optimizer picks it. Once you recognize "small subset of a big table, queried constantly," a filtered index should be one of the first tools you reach for.

To ground this in something familiar: imagine a to-do list app used by an entire company, where every task ever created — including ones completed years ago — lives in one giant table. The screen everyone actually looks at is "my open tasks," which might be 30 rows out of 2 million historical tasks across the whole company. A normal index on a "completed" flag doesn't help nearly as much as you'd hope, because the optimizer knows a huge fraction of rows could match either value, and a scan starts looking cheaper than expected. A filtered index — one built specifically over just the incomplete tasks — sidesteps that entirely: it's a small, dedicated structure containing only the handful of rows anyone is actually looking at moment to moment, and it stays small and fast regardless of how many millions of completed, no-longer-interesting tasks pile up in the background. This is a genuinely common pattern worth internalizing as a general shape, not just a specific fix: whenever a system distinguishes between "active" and "archived/settled" data, and the active subset is a small fraction of the whole, a filtered index targeted at exactly that active subset is very often the cleanest, cheapest possible fix — cheaper in both storage and maintenance than indexing the entire table, and dramatically more effective for the queries people actually run all day.

One caveat worth flagging: filtered indexes interact with query parameterization in a way that's easy to trip over -- if a query's filter is written with a parameter instead of a literal value (e.g., WHERE Status = @status), SQL Server sometimes can't prove at compile time that the parameter will always match the filtered index's condition, and may decline to use it. This is why filtered indexes tend to work best and most predictably for fixed, well-known conditions like a specific status value, rather than fully dynamic, parameterized filters.

## Scenario
A fulfillment dashboard runs `SELECT ... FROM Orders WHERE Status = 'Pending'` constantly. Only ~1% of the 400k rows are `Pending`, but the query does a full **Clustered Index Scan** — it reads all 400k rows to find ~4k.

## Why it's slow
There is no index supporting the `Status` predicate, so SQL Server scans the whole table. A normal index on `Status` would work, but its key would be dominated by the 396k `'Completed'` rows you never query — wasted space and maintenance.

## What to look for
- A **Clustered Index Scan** on `Orders` reading far more rows than the query returns.

## The concept
A **filtered index** indexes only the rows matching a predicate: `CREATE INDEX ... ON Orders(Status) WHERE Status = 'Pending'`. It is tiny (a few thousand rows), so the seek is fast and the index is cheap to maintain. Add `INCLUDE` columns to cover the query and avoid key lookups. Filtered indexes are ideal for skewed columns where you only query the rare values (open orders, soft-deleted flags, error states).
startingQuery: SELECT OrderId, CustomerId, Total FROM Orders WHERE Status = 'Pending';
hints: The plan scans all 400k rows but returns ~4k — you need an index on Status.
A full index on Status wastes space on the 99% 'Completed' rows you never filter for.
Create a FILTERED index: CREATE NONCLUSTERED INDEX IX_Orders_Pending ON Orders(Status) INCLUDE (CustomerId, Total) WHERE Status = 'Pending';
